extracted.intended_audience: voters/ratifiers of the proposed U.S. Constitution; legislators and civic leaders (People of the State of New York)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and standards for constituting the executive appointment process and the federal judiciary: who appoints, tenure and support of judges, scope of judicial power, and institutional safeguards for independence and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of the Senate with the President in appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointments should involve the President (nomination) joined with the Senate (approval), creating a joint mechanism for filling offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This union prevents undue influence from either side: nomination by the Executive with Senate consent produces accountability (bad nominations blamed on the President; unjust rejections blamed on the Senate). It yields the benefits of appointment while avoiding its evils that would arise from sole executive appointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: President nominates; Senate confirms (nomination subject to Senate control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of nomination vested unequivocally in the Executive, with each nomination submitted to the judgment of an entire branch of the legislature (the Senate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting nominations to a full legislative branch renders appointment circumstances matters of public notoriety and assigns clear responsibility: the President for nominating, the Senate for approving or rejecting. This transparency mitigates secretive patronage and cabal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of small private councils for appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: A small, closed council of appointment (e.g., 3–5 persons) is inappropriate for distributing public offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: secrecy, impenetrability to public eye, ease of cabal and intrigue, barter of votes, monopolization of offices, and lack of public accountability. Such councils tend toward favoritism, instability (if membership rotates), and greater susceptibility to executive influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Representatives unsuitable for appointment power
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniting the House of Representatives with appointment power is unfit because the House is numerous and fluctuating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large, changeable body would defeat stability advantages of the Executive and Senate in appointments and introduce infinite delays and embarrassments; example: in half a century the House might number hundreds, making it improper for exercise of appointment power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated executive powers (limited list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive's remaining powers include informing Congress of the state of the Union; recommending measures; convening either branch on extraordinary occasions; adjourning when branches disagree on adjournment; receiving ambassadors; faithfully executing the laws; and commissioning all officers of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the narrowly described authorities of the Executive; objections to these powers are minor or unsubstantial. The power to convene the Senate is justified by the need to address treaties without convening the House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure of judges: hold during good behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: All judges appointed by the United States should hold their offices during good behavior (i.e., life tenure contingent on good behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life tenure is derived from State constitutions and is recommended to secure a steady, upright, and impartial administration of the laws; it is a barrier against encroachments by other branches and aids judicial firmness and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence as essential safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary must be independent because from the nature of its functions it is the least dangerous but most vulnerable branch and must be able to defend itself against the other departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence requires permanency in office and secure compensation. Without these, the judiciary could be overawed or influenced by the Executive or Legislature; separation of powers (judging distinct from lawmaking/executing) is necessary for liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts have the right to declare legislative acts void
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial tribunals must have the authority to declare legislative acts void when they are contrary to the Constitution because every act of a delegated authority contrary to its commission is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power does not imply judicial superiority over the legislature; rather it recognizes the Constitution as superior to ordinary statutes and assigns courts the role of ascertaining constitutional meaning. Example: when statute and constitution irreconcilably conflict, the constitution controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts as intermediaries between the people and the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are intended to be an intermediate body to keep the legislature within constitutional limits and to prefer fundamental law over statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts; judges should regulate decisions by the Constitution rather than conflicting statutory law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency in office and fixed provision for judicial support
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanency in office (life tenure) and a fixed provision for judicial support (compensation that shall not be diminished during continuance in office) are necessary to secure judicial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation may be adjusted to reflect changes in value of money, but the legislature must be prohibited from diminishing a judge's pay while in office. This prevents legislative power over subsistence from becoming power over will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment as the appropriate responsibility mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should be liable to impeachment by the House and tried by the Senate for misconduct; conviction may lead to dismissal and disqualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the only provision consistent with necessary judicial independence; it balances responsibility (removal for malconduct) without subjecting judges to routine removal that would undermine independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against removal for inability / age limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions to remove judges for inability (e.g., fixed retirement age) are inadvisable because measuring mental faculties is impractical and liable to abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: arbitrary age limits (e.g., New York's rule excluding judges beyond sixty) are criticized as unjust and unnecessary; insanity can be addressed as a de facto disqualification without broad, vulnerable removal mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for long tenure to build legal expertise and precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluminous code of laws and the weight of precedents demand long and laborious study; therefore, life tenure attracts and retains the limited number of men fit for the bench.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary commissions discourage skilled practitioners from accepting judicial office, likely resulting in less able judges and poorer administration of justice. Precedent accumulation requires continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal judicial jurisdiction categories (scope of federal courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal judiciary ought to extend to: (1) cases arising under laws of the United States; (2) cases concerning execution of the articles of Union; (3) cases in which the United States are a party; (4) cases involving the peace of the Confederacy (foreign or interstate intercourse); (5) causes originating on the high seas (admiralty/maritime); and (6) cases where state tribunals cannot be supposed impartial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: to give efficacy to constitutional provisions (1); uniformity of interpretation of national laws (2); propriety and decorum for controversies involving the nation (3); preserving the peace of the whole (4); specialized maritime jurisdiction (5); and ensuring impartial adjudication when state courts are biased (6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts necessary to enforce constitutional limits on states
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a constitutional method for giving efficacy to restrictions on State legislatures; federal courts provide the authority to overrule state laws that contravene the articles of Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative (a direct negative on state laws) was possible but the convention chose federal courts to overrule state statutes inconsistent with national provisions. Without such a mechanism prohibitions on state action would be ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of interpretation of national laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in interpreting national laws requires federal tribunals of final jurisdiction rather than multiple independent state courts of final jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing many independent final courts over the same national laws would produce contradiction and confusion (a 'hydra' in government); a single coherent national judicial structure avoids that risk.
